seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 167 HTS Chapter 12 lines: soybeans, peanuts, canola, flax, sunflower, sesame and hemp seed, vegetable and grass seed for sowing, hops, ginseng, psyllium, seaweed, hay and alfalfa. General, FTA and Column 2 rates plus the extra duty by country.

overview.intro:
Chapter 12 covers oil seeds and almost everything else farmers plant or feed that is not a cereal: soybeans, peanuts, flax, canola, sunflower, sesame, mustard and hemp seed; vegetable, flower and grass **seed for sowing**; hops; ginseng, psyllium and other medicinal plants; seaweed, carob and sugar beet; and straw, hay and alfalfa. Of its **167 tariff lines**, 82 are Free at the general rate and most others pay a few cents per kilogram. The exception is **raw peanuts outside the tariff-rate quota: 131.8%, or 163.8% in the shell**.

The extra duty by country matters more. The U.S. imported **$2.67B** of Chapter 12 goods in 2025; Canada supplied 27%, mostly soybeans, hay, canola, flax and mustard, and USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff** (+10% for India and Argentina, 10% in total for the EU, up to 37.5% for China and Brazil), but **seeds for sowing are exempt**: 74 lines, including all of heading 1209. Since **August 22, 2026**, 42 lines from Canada, among them many vegetable and flower seeds, hops, mint, seaweed and herbs, pay a **50% Section 338 duty even with a USMCA claim**.

productGroups.label: Soybeans
productGroups.blurb: Free for every line, seed or not. Canada ($190M) and Argentina ($92M) were the largest suppliers in 2025. Seed soybeans are on the Section 301 exemption list; other soybeans pay the 2026 extra duty for most of the 60 economies (10% for Argentina).

productGroups.label: Peanuts (groundnuts), raw
productGroups.blurb: A tariff-rate quota: in-quota peanuts pay 6.6¢/kg (9.35¢/kg in shell); over-quota peanuts pay 131.8% (163.8% in shell) and may owe a further agricultural safeguard duty. Mexico and FTA partners enter free. Imports were only $5.2M in 2025.

productGroups.label: Copra
productGroups.blurb: Free and on both the Section 301 and the Brazil exemption lists. Imports are negligible ($11,000 in 2025).

productGroups.label: Flaxseed (linseed)
productGroups.blurb: 0.39¢/kg. Canada supplied $72M of the $87M imported in 2025; flaxseed for sowing is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Rapeseed & canola
productGroups.blurb: 0.58¢/kg on canola (low erucic acid) and other rapeseed. Canada shipped $91M of the $114M imported in 2025, and USMCA makes it Free.

productGroups.label: Sunflower seeds
productGroups.blurb: Free. Bulgaria ($78M) and Canada ($23M) lead; EU sunflower seeds now pay 10% in total under the 2026 Section 301 rule for the EU, except seeds for sowing.

productGroups.label: Sesame, mustard, hemp, cotton, melon, poppy & other oil seeds
productGroups.blurb: Mostly Free: sesame, mustard, safflower, castor, palm nuts, niger and hemp seed. Cottonseed is 0.47¢/kg, melon seeds 0.83¢/kg, poppy seeds 0.06¢/kg. $412M in 2025; Paraguay shipped $87M of other oil seeds (1207.99), India $40M of sesame, Canada $57M of mustard.

productGroups.label: Flours & meals of oil seeds
productGroups.blurb: Soy flour 1.9%, other oilseed flours and meals 1.4%. Certified organic soy flour and meal from India is also under antidumping and countervailing duty orders.

productGroups.label: Seeds for sowing (vegetable, flower, grass & forage)
productGroups.blurb: The chapter's biggest heading: $562M in 2025, $374M of it vegetable seed. Base rates run from Free to 5.9¢/kg (cauliflower). Every line is on the Section 301 exemption list, but many Canadian seed lines pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

productGroups.label: Hop cones, hop pellets & lupulin
productGroups.blurb: 13.2¢/kg on hop cones and pellets. Germany shipped $25M of the $51M imported in 2025. EU hops pay 10% in total; Canadian hops pay an extra 50% under Section 338, even with a USMCA claim.

productGroups.label: Medicinal & herbal plants (ginseng, psyllium, mint)
productGroups.blurb: Mostly Free: ginseng roots, psyllium husk, basil, sage, herbal teas and other botanicals. Chilled or frozen herbs are 6%, processed mint 4.8%, tonka beans 6.6¢/kg. $511M in 2025, led by India ($152M) and Mexico ($63M). Coca leaf and poppy straw need DEA permits.

productGroups.label: Seaweed, carob, sugar beet & cane, fruit kernels
productGroups.blurb: Seaweed, carob, chicory root and most other lines are Free; sugar beet is 39.7¢/t, sugar cane $1.24/t and fruit kernels 1.5¢/kg. China supplied $94M of the $229M imported in 2025.

productGroups.label: Cereal straw & husks
productGroups.blurb: Free. $13M in 2025, almost all from Canada. Straw from foot-and-mouth disease regions must be treated or quarantined.

productGroups.label: Hay, alfalfa & forage
productGroups.blurb: Hay and forage are Free; alfalfa meal and pellets 1.4%. Canada shipped $106M of the $121M imported in 2025; USMCA-qualifying hay and cubes enter free.

workedExamples.title: A $500,000 cargo of Argentine soybeans
workedExamples.body: Soybeans are Free at the general rate, but Argentina is one of the 60 economies in the 2026 Section 301 action, so 10% of value is added (9903.05.22): **$50,000**. Canadian soybeans with a USMCA claim pay **$0** (9903.05.93), and Ukrainian or Paraguayan soybeans, from countries outside the 60, pay nothing at all.

workedExamples.title: Vegetable seed from Canada: USMCA no longer makes it free
workedExamples.body: Tomato seed for sowing is 1.5¢/kg, Free under USMCA, and on the Section 301 exemption list. But 1209.91.80 is on the Section 338 list for Canada (U.S. note 51(b)(3), 9903.03.14), and that **50%** applies even when USMCA is claimed. On a $40,000 shipment of seed the duty is **$20,000**. The same seed from the Netherlands or Chile pays only its base rate (Chile: Free under the FTA).

workedExamples.title: 5 tonnes of German hop pellets
workedExamples.body: Hop pellets are 13.2¢/kg: 5,000 kg × $0.132 = $660. For EU goods whose base rate is under 10% of value, the 2026 Section 301 action charges **10% in total in place of the base rate** (9903.05.39). At $15/kg the lot is worth $75,000, so the duty is **$7,500**. Canadian hop pellets pay the base rate plus 50% under Section 338 (9903.03.13) plus 10% unless they qualify for USMCA.

workedExamples.title: Psyllium husk from India
workedExamples.body: Psyllium seed husks are Free at the general rate. Indian goods pay the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.44): **$3,000** on a $30,000 container. Psyllium husks from Malaysia, Cambodia, Guatemala, Argentina, Bangladesh, Taiwan and Jordan are exempt when declared as such (U.S. note 52(j)), but India has no exception list.

Heading 1209 does not, however, apply to the following even if for sowing: (a) leguminous vegetables or sweet corn (chapter 7); (b) spices or other products of chapter 9; (c) cereals (chapter 10); or (d) products of headings 1201 to 1207 or of heading 1211.

**Note 4.** Heading 1211 applies, inter alia, to the following plants or parts thereof: basil, borage, ginseng, hyssop, licorice, all species of mint, rosemary, rue, sage and wormwood. Heading 1211 does not, however, apply to: (a) medicaments of chapter 30; (b) perfumery, cosmetic or toilet preparations of chapter 33; or (c) insecticides, fungicides, herbicides, disinfectants or similar products of heading 3808.

**Note 5.** For the purposes of heading 1212, the term "seaweeds and other algae" does not include: (a) dead single-cell microorganisms of heading 2102; (b) cultures of microorganisms of heading 3002; or (c) fertilizers of heading 3101 or 3105.

seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 12 since January 2025: base rates on all 167 lines, the end of the IEEPA duties and the Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and their seed exemption, and the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian seeds and hops, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). The base rates of all 161 lines that exist in both are unchanged; six lines are new statistical splits (organic and other hemp seed, oil seeds and botanicals) added on July 1, 2026, all Free.

The changes came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**, but 74 seed and other lines are exempt. China pays up to **37.5%** and Brazil **37.5%** because other Section 301 duties stack. And since **August 22, 2026**, 42 lines from **Canada**, many of them seeds, hops and herbs, pay a **50% Section 338 duty that a USMCA claim does not remove**.

changes.title: No Chapter 12 base-rate changes; six new statistical lines
changes.detail: Every Chapter 12 line that exists in both editions carries the same General, FTA and Column 2 rate in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Six 10-digit lines are new: Revision 11 (in force July 1, 2026) split hemp seed not for sowing into certified organic (1207.99.03.65) and other (.75), other oil seeds into certified organic (.92) and other (.97), and other botanicals of 1211.90.89 into certified organic (.92) and other (.97). All are Free, as before.

changes.title: Canada import bans list no Chapter 12 line
changes.detail: Proclamations of September 8, 2026 banned some Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles from September 29. The dairy ban covers whey, molasses and non-alcoholic beer, not the hop pellets on the dairy duty list, so Chapter 12 goods can still be imported; the 42 lines on the Section 338 lists keep paying 50%.

changes.title: New federal hemp definition delayed to December 11, 2026
changes.detail: The FY2026 Agriculture appropriations law (P.L. 119-37, enacted November 12, 2025) narrows the definition of hemp to a total-THC limit of 0.3% and excludes viable seeds from a cannabis plant above that limit, which would make them marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act. A continuing resolution passed September 2, 2026 (P.L. 119-103) delays most of the new definition to December 11, 2026. It affects hemp seed for sowing (1207.99.03.40); the tariff rate (Free) is unchanged.

changes.title: Section 338 duty of 50% on 42 Canadian seed, hop and herb lines
changes.detail: Proclamations of July 20, 2026 put a 50% duty on listed products of Canada; after a short suspension it took effect August 22. The lists in U.S. note 51 include hop pellets (9903.03.13) and, under 9903.03.14, most vegetable, flower, beet, white clover and tree seed for sowing, hop cones, mint, herbs and other plants of 1211.90, food seaweed, carob and 1212.99.92. The duty applies on top of the base rate and the Section 301 duty, and also to USMCA-qualifying goods (note 51(a)). Proclamation 11065 changed the 9903.03.14 list from September 15, 2026 without adding or removing a Chapter 12 line.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies; seeds for sowing exempt
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), on 93 of the 167 Chapter 12 lines. 74 of the 167 lines are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) and pay no 2026 Section 301 duty: every seed line of heading 1209, plus seed soybeans, seed peanuts, copra, and flaxseed, rapeseed, sunflower and cotton seed for sowing, melon seeds and poppy seeds. Castor, sesame, mustard, safflower and other 1207.99 seeds (including hemp seed) are also exempt when entered for sowing and declared as such (note 52(c), 9903.05.87). EU goods pay 10% in total and Japan and South Korea 12.5% in total. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). The exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) covers only copra and poppy seeds in Chapter 12, so Brazilian seeds for sowing pay the 25%. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on the non-exempt lines.

changes.title: Organic statistical lines for hemp seed, oil seeds and botanicals
changes.detail: Revision 11 split 1207.99.03.60 (hemp seed, other) and .91 (other oil seeds) and 1211.90.89.90 (other botanicals) into certified organic and other statistical lines. The rate, Free, did not change.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) on Canadian and Mexican goods still apply.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing duties on organic soybean meal from India continue
changes.detail: The 2022 orders on certified organic soybean meal from India name 1208.10.00.10 (organic soy flour and meal) as well as 2304.00. After the latest reviews (January 23 and February 26, 2026) the antidumping cash deposit is 18.80% for Tejawat Organic Foods and 3.07% for all others, and countervailing rates are 3.66% to 75.48% for the reviewed firms (9.57% for all others from the order). These are collected on top of the 1.9% base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Only copra (1203.00) and poppy seeds (1207.91) were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); soybeans, seeds for sowing, hops and herbs paid it. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Extra 25% duty on Indian goods removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India tied to purchases of Russian oil (9903.01.84–9903.01.89), for goods entered from February 7, 2026. India's reciprocal duty ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) is listed on most dutiable Chapter 12 lines, including in-quota peanuts, but not on the over-quota peanut lines. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 tariff scheduled for 2027 and 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a tariff on products of Nicaragua that is 0% until the end of 2026, then +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01). It applies only to goods that do not claim a special rate such as CAFTA-DR, and it reaches all 167 Chapter 12 lines, seeds included. Nicaragua also pays the 12.5% 2026 forced-labor tariff (9903.05.58) on non-exempt lines.

changes.title: Farm-goods exemption reached only copra and poppy seeds
changes.detail: The exemption list for the reciprocal duties (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a), heading 9903.01.32), widened for agricultural products from November 13, 2025, named only two Chapter 12 subheadings: copra (1203.00) and poppy seeds (1207.91). Soybeans, seeds, hops, herbs and hay stayed subject to the reciprocal duties until they ended on February 24, 2026.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: Extra 25% duty on Indian goods
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on products of India, on top of the reciprocal duty, because India was importing Russian oil. It covered Indian psyllium, sesame and seeds. Removed February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: APHIS restores its pre-2020 rules for genetically engineered seed
changes.detail: A federal court vacated APHIS's 2020 biotechnology rule on December 2, 2024, and APHIS conformed 7 CFR part 340 to the earlier regulations. Importing a regulated genetically engineered organism, such as unapproved GE seed, again needs an APHIS permit or notification under those rules.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 12 goods were **$2.67B in 2025**, down 9.1% from $2.94B in 2024 and 24% below the 2022 peak of $3.52B. Four groups make up most of it.

**Seeds for sowing ($562M, 21%)**, $374M of it vegetable seed, come from Canada ($78M), the Netherlands ($71M), Chile ($41M), India ($39M), France ($36M) and Denmark ($30M). **Medicinal and herbal plants ($511M)** are led by India ($152M, the line that includes psyllium husk) and Mexico ($63M).

**Soybeans ($424M)** come mainly from Canada ($190M) and Argentina ($92M), with Ukraine ($50M, up from almost nothing in 2024), Russia ($37M) and Türkiye ($31M) behind. **Other oil seeds ($412M)** include Paraguay's $87M of 1207.99, Canadian mustard ($57M) and Indian sesame ($40M). The total rate on Chapter 12 goods depends far more on **where they come from** than on the printed rate, which is Free or a few cents per kilogram on most lines. Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.
Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; CL for Chile. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.

Conditional relief is not applied (it needs the importer's confirmation): 9903.05.87 (Section 301), 9903.06.01 (Section 301), 9903.06.03 (Section 301), 9903.06.05 (Section 301), 9903.06.11 (Section 301), 9903.06.13 (Section 301), 9903.06.15 (Section 301), 9903.06.21 (Section 301).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

Castor, sesame, mustard, safflower and other 1207.99 seeds for sowing are exempt only when declared as such (9903.05.87), so their cells show the duty.

Canada: the 50% Section 338 duty (U.S. note 51) is charged on its 42 listed lines on both the USMCA and non-USMCA sides; it does not apply to goods properly entered under Chapter 98 or to personal baggage. The September 29, 2026 Canadian import bans list no Chapter 12 line.

Over-quota peanuts (131.8%, 163.8%) can also owe the special agricultural safeguard duty of 9904.12.01–9904.12.19 when a safeguard period is in effect; it is not in the cells.

Antidumping and countervailing duties are not in the cells: certified organic soybean meal and flour from India (1208.10.00.10) owes both (3.07% antidumping and 9.57% countervailing for most exporters). No federal excise tax applies to Chapter 12 goods.

seo.shortDescription: The permits, certificates and rules for each HTS Chapter 12 line (APHIS plants-for-planting and khapra beetle rules, Federal Seed Act, FDA prior notice, USDA organic and peanut rules, DEA and CITES) and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTA claims, the seed exemption, the peanut quota, Chapter 98 and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For Chapter 12 the paperwork depends on whether the goods will be **planted, eaten or fed**. Seed for sowing goes through USDA APHIS plants-for-planting rules and the Federal Seed Act. Soybeans, oil seeds, herbs, seaweed and hay for food or feed need FDA prior notice, a registered foreign facility and an importer with a Foreign Supplier Verification Program. Some goods add their own gate: khapra-beetle declarations for soybeans and safflower from countries such as India, APHIS permits for cottonseed and sugarcane, USDA quality rules for peanuts, DEA permits for coca leaf and poppy straw, CITES papers for ginseng.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another **FTA**, enter genuine **seed for sowing** under the exempt lines, bring peanuts in **within the quota**, use a **Chapter 98** provision when the purpose fits, or claim **drawback** on goods that are exported. None of them removes the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian seed, hops and herbs.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty (10% of value) plus any base rate, such as 0.58¢/kg on canola, 13.2¢/kg on hops or 131.8% on over-quota peanuts
levers.appliesTo: All 167 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA. On the 42 Canadian Section 338 lines it removes only the base rate and the 10%, not the 50%.
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Claiming without a valid certification exposes the entry to the 10% Section 301 duty plus penalties. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

levers.title: Claim an FTA or AGOA rate on the base duty
levers.saves: The base rate: Free instead of up to 163.8% (over-quota peanuts in the shell), 13.2¢/kg (hops) or 6% (frozen herbs). The Section 301 duty for the country still applies.
levers.appliesTo: The 85 dutiable lines, for goods originating in an FTA partner (for example Chile, Peru, Colombia, Australia, South Korea, Israel, CAFTA-DR countries) or an AGOA country
levers.document: The origin documentation the agreement requires, with the special program indicator (CL, PE, CO, AU, KR, IL, P, D …) on the entry.
levers.caveat: FTA and AGOA claims do not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). AGOA does not cover over-quota peanuts. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020. AGOA runs through December 31, 2026.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Enter genuine seed for sowing under the seed lines, and declare it
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5% of value, or the EU's 10% in place of the base rate) for the 60 economies
levers.appliesTo: All of heading 1209 and the sowing lines of soybeans, peanuts, flax, rapeseed, sunflower and cotton seed (9903.05.86); castor, sesame, mustard, safflower and other 1207.99 seeds (including hemp) for sowing when declared (9903.05.87)
levers.document: The APHIS phytosanitary certificate or permit and the Federal Seed Act declaration and container labels (see the rules below); for 9903.05.87, the entry declares the seed is for sowing.
levers.caveat: Only seed really used for sowing qualifies. China (List 3 or 4A), Brazil (25%) and, for 42 Canadian lines, Section 338 (50%) still charge their duties on seed.

levers.title: Bring peanuts in within the tariff-rate quota
levers.saves: The over-quota rate: 6.6¢/kg instead of 131.8% (shelled, seed), or 9.35¢/kg instead of 163.8% (in shell), and any safeguard duty
levers.appliesTo: Peanuts of heading 1202 from countries without a free FTA rate, such as Argentina (43,901 t a year) and other countries (9,005 t), April 1 to March 31
levers.document: An entry under the in-quota subheading (1202.30.40, 1202.41.40, 1202.42.15 or 1202.42.60); CBP fixes quota priority when the entry summary is presented.
levers.caveat: The quota fills on a first-come basis by entry time; once it is full, further peanuts pay the over-quota rate. Peanuts for human consumption must also meet USDA quality and aflatoxin standards.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the purpose fits
levers.saves: The base rate, the 2026 Section 301 duty and the Canada Section 338 duty: each provision below is Free in the schedule
levers.appliesTo: Goods imported for a specific purpose, whatever their Chapter 12 line
levers.document: Evidence of the qualifying purpose: proof of U.S. origin and export for returned goods (19 CFR 10.1), or a bond for samples and test lots.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) and the Section 338 duties do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision, except entries under 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. notes 51(a), 52(a)). The entry must qualify, so get CBP's agreement (or a ruling) before relying on it.

provisions.text: U.S. goods returned after export without being advanced in value or improved in condition, for example a rejected soybean or seed cargo
Samples solely for use in taking orders
Articles solely for testing, experimental or review purposes, for example a trial lot of seed or hops

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(a)

levers.title: Claim drawback on goods that are exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties, taxes and fees paid on imported goods that are later exported or destroyed, or on substituted goods of the same 8-digit line
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for importers or processors (crushers, seed companies, brewers) that also export
levers.document: A drawback claim filed electronically with CBP, with import and export records linking the two; for substitution, records showing the exported goods are classifiable under the same 8-digit subheading.
levers.caveat: Drawback has strict time limits (5 years from import) and record-keeping rules. Check with CBP which Chapter 99 duties are refundable for your claim.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (seed for sowing or oil stock, raw or processed herb, Chapter 12 or a preparation of Chapter 20 or 21) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate or the exemption
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the goods, their processing and their intended use. Questions about whether goods fall inside an antidumping order go to Commerce as a scope ruling.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different shipment may need its own.

rules.title: Prior notice of imported food and animal feed: file before the goods arrive
Food facility registration for foreign processors, packers and warehouses that handle the goods (farms are exempt)
Foreign Supplier Verification Program: the U.S. importer must verify each foreign supplier of food or feed
Seed for planting: phytosanitary certificate naming the genus (or an APHIS permit for small lots), port inspection, and the restrictions on specific plant types

Imported agricultural and vegetable seed: importer's declaration of kind, variety, origin and use, labels on each container, noxious-weed seed limits; coated or pelleted seed needs a sample drawn before coating
Genetically engineered seed or plants that are regulated articles: APHIS permit or notification before import (pre-2020 rules restored June 16, 2025)

Khapra-beetle countries (including India): soybeans and safflower seeds need a phytosanitary certificate declaring the shipment inspected and found free of khapra beetle and may not come in passenger baggage; melon and other cucurbit seeds not for planting (over 2 ounces) must be treated
Cottonseed and cottonseed hulls: import prohibited unless under an APHIS permit and the cotton regulations (pink bollworm)
Sugarcane, including cuttings, canes, leaves and bagasse: prohibited from all foreign countries except under a controlled import permit
Rice straw and hulls need an APHIS permit and inspection; straw of wheat and other Karnal-bunt hosts is restricted
Hay and straw: free entry only from regions free of foot-and-mouth disease; otherwise held in quarantine for at least 90 days or treated
Imported peanuts: entry data to CBP before arrival, then inspection and a negative aflatoxin certificate before use for human consumption
Certified organic lines: each shipment needs NOP Import Certificate data entered in CBP's ACE and organic marking on the import documents
Coca leaf and opium poppy straw are Schedule II controlled substances: DEA registration and an import permit before shipment

Hemp seed: must be hemp (no more than 0.3% THC) to stay outside the Controlled Substances Act; from December 11, 2026 viable seed above 0.3% total THC is excluded from hemp. Seed for sowing also follows the APHIS seed rules
Ephedra: dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids are adulterated and may not be sold
CITES-listed plants: American ginseng roots are in Appendix II and need CITES documents; check other botanicals against the CITES appendices before shipping
Antidumping and countervailing duties on certified organic soybean meal from India: cash deposits at entry (3.07% AD and 9.57% CVD for most exporters)

groups.label: Soybeans
groups.note: Seed soybeans (1201.10) follow the APHIS seed and Federal Seed Act rules; soybeans for crushing or food follow the FDA rules. Soybeans from khapra-beetle countries need the khapra declaration either way.

groups.label: Peanuts (groundnuts), raw
groups.note: Seed peanuts follow the seed rules; other peanuts the FDA rules and the USDA quality and aflatoxin standards. The quota of Additional U.S. Note 2 decides the rate.

groups.label: Copra
groups.note: Copra follows the FDA food and feed rules.

groups.label: Flaxseed (linseed)
groups.note: Flaxseed for sowing (1204.00.00.10) follows the seed rules; flax for oil or food the FDA rules.

groups.label: Rapeseed & canola
groups.note: Canola and rapeseed for sowing follow the seed rules and, for regulated GE varieties, 7 CFR part 340; seed for crushing follows the FDA rules.

groups.label: Sunflower seeds
groups.note: Sunflower seed for sowing (1206.00.00.31) follows the seed rules; snack and oil-stock seeds the FDA rules.

groups.label: Sesame, mustard, hemp, cotton, melon, poppy & other oil seeds
groups.note: Cottonseed needs an APHIS permit; safflower and melon seeds from khapra-beetle countries need the khapra declaration or treatment; hemp seed must meet the hemp THC limit.

groups.label: Flours & meals of oil seeds
groups.note: Oilseed flours follow the FDA rules. Certified organic soy flour and meal from India owes antidumping and countervailing deposits.

groups.label: Seeds for sowing (vegetable, flower, grass & forage)
groups.note: Every line is seed for sowing: phytosanitary certificate or permit, Federal Seed Act declaration and labels, and the 7 CFR 319.37-20 restrictions for specific plant types. No FDA prior notice for seed that is only for planting.

groups.label: Hop cones, hop pellets & lupulin
groups.note: Hops for brewing follow the FDA food rules.

groups.label: Medicinal & herbal plants (ginseng, psyllium, mint)
groups.note: Herbs, psyllium and ginseng for food or supplements follow the FDA rules; coca leaf and poppy straw need DEA permits; ginseng roots need CITES documents; ephedra cannot go into dietary supplements.

groups.label: Seaweed, carob, sugar beet & cane, fruit kernels
groups.note: Seaweed, carob and kernels follow the FDA rules; sugarcane is prohibited except under an APHIS controlled import permit.

groups.label: Cereal straw & husks
groups.note: Straw must come from a foot-and-mouth-free region or be quarantined or treated; rice straw and hulls need an APHIS permit.

groups.label: Hay, alfalfa & forage
groups.note: Hay, alfalfa and forage are animal feed: FDA prior notice and FSVP apply, and hay from foot-and-mouth disease regions is quarantined or treated.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing oil seeds, seeds for sowing, herbs, hops and hay into the U.S.: tariffs by country, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Most Chapter 12 goods are Free or a few cents per kilogram at the general rate; raw peanuts over the quota (131.8%, 163.8% in the shell) are the exception.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: +10% for India and Argentina, 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% for Chile, up to 37.5% for China and Brazil. Seeds for sowing (74 lines) are exempt.

USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free, except 42 Canadian lines, mostly vegetable and flower seed, hops and herbs, which pay a 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026 even with USMCA.

faqs.question: Is there a U.S. tariff on soybeans?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on soybeans
faqs.answer: The base rate on soybeans (1201) is Free. Since July 24, 2026 soybeans other than seed from 60 economies pay a Section 301 tariff: 10% for Argentina, 12.5% for Türkiye, 10% in total for the EU and 37.5% for China and Brazil. Seed soybeans (1201.10) are exempt. USMCA-qualifying soybeans from Canada pay nothing, and soybeans from countries outside the 60, such as Ukraine and Paraguay, pay nothing. China's own tariffs on U.S. soybean exports are a separate question.

faqs.question: Does the U.S. import soybeans, and from where?
searchedAs: how much soybean does us import
does the us import soybeans from brazil
faqs.answer: Yes, a small amount for a major exporter: $424M of soybeans in 2025, $411M of it for crushing or food. Canada supplied $190M, Argentina $92M, Ukraine $50M, Russia $37M and Türkiye $31M. Brazil shipped none in 2025, and China $2.2M.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for soybeans?
faqs.answer: Heading 1201. Seed soybeans are 1201.10.00.00; other soybeans are 1201.90.00, split into oil stock (.05), certified organic (.10) and other (.90). All are Free at the general rate. Soy flour is 1208.10, soybean oil 1507 and soybean meal 2304, outside this heading.

faqs.question: Can I import seeds into the U.S.?
searchedAs: can i import seeds into the us
can i bring seeds to usa
faqs.answer: Yes, if they meet USDA rules. Seed for planting needs a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country that names the genus, or an APHIS permit for small lots of up to 50 packets (7 CFR 319.37-5, 319.37-6), and some plant types are restricted (319.37-20). Agricultural and vegetable seed also needs the importer's Federal Seed Act declaration and labels on each container (7 CFR 361.3). Regulated genetically engineered seed needs an APHIS permit or notification.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for seeds for sowing and vegetable seeds?
faqs.answer: Heading 1209 covers seeds of a kind used for sowing: sugar beet (1209.10), forage and grass seed such as alfalfa, clover, fescue, bluegrass and ryegrass (1209.21–1209.29), flower seed (1209.30), vegetable seed (1209.91) and tree and other seed (1209.99). Seed of cereals, beans and oil seeds stays in its own heading (Chapter 12 Note 3), for example seed soybeans in 1201.10.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on imported seeds?
faqs.answer: Base rates on seed for sowing run from Free to 5.9¢/kg (cauliflower). All 60 lines of heading 1209 are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariff, but Chinese seed still pays 25% or 7.5% under the older China lists, Brazilian seed 25%, and 42 Canadian lines, including most vegetable and flower seed, pay 50% under Section 338 even with a USMCA claim. Seed from the Netherlands, Chile, India or France pays only the base rate.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for hemp seed?
faqs.answer: 1207.99.03: hemp seed for sowing is 1207.99.03.40, and other hemp seed is certified organic (1207.99.03.65) or other (1207.99.03.75). All are Free. CBP has classified hulled hemp seeds in the same subheading (ruling N319371, 2021). Hemp seed oil is not in Chapter 12. From December 11, 2026 viable seed above 0.3% total THC no longer counts as hemp.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for sesame seeds?
faqs.answer: 1207.40.00, split into certified organic (.10) and other (.90). The general rate is Free. Sesame from India pays the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.44) and from China 37.5%; sesame entered and declared for sowing is exempt (9903.05.87). India shipped $40M of sesame in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for hops?
faqs.answer: Hop cones are 1210.10 and hop pellets, ground hops and lupulin 1210.20, both 13.2¢/kg. German and other EU hops pay 10% of value in total (9903.05.39). Canadian hops pay an extra 50% under Section 338 (9903.03.13 for pellets, 9903.03.14 for cones), even with USMCA. Hop extract is not in Chapter 12.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for psyllium husk?
faqs.answer: Psyllium seed husks are 1211.90.89.20, Free at the general rate. Psyllium from India pays the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.44). Psyllium husks from Malaysia, Cambodia, Guatemala, Argentina, Bangladesh, Taiwan and Jordan are exempt when declared as such (U.S. note 52(j)). India shipped $152M of 1211.90 herbs and plants in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for ginseng root?
faqs.answer: Fresh or dried ginseng roots are 1211.20.10 (cultivated .20, wild .90), Free; chilled or frozen roots are 1211.20.15, 6%. Chinese ginseng roots pay 37.5% more (List 3 plus the 2026 action). American ginseng roots are in CITES Appendix II and need CITES documents (50 CFR 23.68). Ginseng extracts, teas and capsules are classified elsewhere.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for seaweed?
faqs.answer: Seaweed fit for human consumption is 1212.21.00 and other seaweed 1212.29.00, both Free. Korean seaweed pays 12.5% in total under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.71); Chinese seaweed 37.5%; Japanese 12.5% in total. Canadian food seaweed pays 50% under Section 338. Seaweed that has been prepared or seasoned may fall in Chapter 20 or 21 instead.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on hay from Canada?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on hay from canada
faqs.answer: Not if it qualifies for USMCA. Hay (1214.90, with alfalfa .10, timothy .18 and other .25) is Free, and alfalfa meal and pellets (1214.10) are 1.4%, Free under USMCA. Hay that does not qualify pays 10% (9903.05.29), or 11.4% for alfalfa meal and pellets. Hay is not on the Section 338 lists. Canada shipped $106M of hay and forage in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on raw peanuts?
faqs.answer: Raw peanuts are heading 1202 and have a tariff-rate quota: within it 6.6¢/kg (shelled or seed) or 9.35¢/kg (in shell); above it 131.8% or 163.8%, plus a possible safeguard duty. The yearly quota from April 1 is 43,901 t for Argentina and 9,005 t for other countries. Mexican and FTA-partner peanuts are Free. Roasted peanuts and peanut butter are in Chapter 20.

faqs.question: Are there U.S. tariffs on canola from Canada?
faqs.answer: Canola is 1205.10, 0.58¢/kg, which USMCA makes Free, and USMCA-qualifying canola pays no Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). Canola that does not qualify pays 0.58¢/kg plus 10% of value (9903.05.29). Canola is not on the Section 338 lists. Canada shipped $91M of canola seed in 2025; China's tariffs on Canadian canola are a separate matter.
